utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Madam Registrar, and good morning, everybody. Could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, madam. For the record, we are sitting pursuant to Rule 15 bis. Judge Stole is unwell. That's the reason for his absence. I also put on record the absence of Accused Popovic. We have already his waiver, which was just last Friday. I think it's today and tomorrow, Mr. Zivanovic. Isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. So composition or presentation: Prosecution, Mr. McCloskey, Mr. Mitchell; Defence teams, I notice the absence of Mr. Sarapa, Mr. Ostojic, and I think that's -- is he here or not, because I can't see -- and Mr. Petrusic. Thank you, Ms. Fauveau. All right. You said you had about an hour left, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I hope to finish in the first session, and if we're lucky, it's an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: When I said "an hour," I also meant approximately, plus or minus the session, so let's proceed. Good morning to you, Mr. Pandurevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And for planning purposes, Mr. Haynes, more or less, your redirect is going to engage us for how many hours?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I hope to finish today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Oh, I see. Okay, that's good. Thank you. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good morning, General.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: A couple of, hopefully, quick things that I forgot to mention. One, you were -- when you testified in direct about the 15th of July, when you came up the stairs towards your office, and Obrenovic's office, you said you saw the duty officer there, but my notes do not reflect you ever identifying the person. Who did you see there as the duty officer on the 15th?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if you have cited and quoted my answer verbatim. As far as I can remember, the door to the office of the duty operations officer was always open. In passing by, I saw a man there, but since I established no contact with him, I had no chance of establishing his identity either.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you saw a man in the duty office, but you don't know who it was?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you don't remember. There's a difference. So back then, you would have remembered, I take it. It was a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was in a hurry. I just had a precursory glance at him, and I didn't want to stop and talk to him. And perhaps we can look in the documents or in the log-book and see who that particular man was on duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, it was, according to the Prosecution, either Dragan Jokic or Drago Nikolic, and as we both know, they don't look much like each other.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's correct that they do not resemble each other. For a time, Mr. Simic -- or at least he was supposed to be on duty that day, but for some reasons he couldn't, but it could have been Mr. Nikolic then. But they do not resemble each other. You just see a figure of a person in passing and you just forget about it afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Another -- something I forgot to ask you about. Do you remember seeing a "Drinski" magazine article about -- out of 1995 about the pig farm for the 4th Battalion?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have seen many articles in the "Drinski" magazine. They wrote about the life in the units and what the soldiers were doing, so that was probably the topic of their reporting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to 65 ter number 4296, then, and this is something that was on our original cross-examination list and you may recognise it. We're going to have to use the computer for this one. So now we can see this article, dated February 1995, entitled "The First Furrow of the War," and there's a picture there of the man they're talking to. Who is that?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is Second Lieutenant Pero Vidakovic, commander of the 4th Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And he was the person that was not in the area during the time of these events, correct, that we're talking about?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And do you remember seeing this article in preparation for your testimony with -- and cross-examination, excuse me, not testimony but cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I perused the documents received for cross-examination. I've seen this article. I didn't read it completely, but I have the gist of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And then I think we left off on Friday with 65 ter 4294, but I don't think we need to get to it. You'll agree with me, I think, that that was a conversation on Saturday, 23 September, where Krstic left a message for you to be there with him on Monday morning, the 25th. Remember that?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to 65 ter number 7D00701, a document that I believe was discussed by you in direct. And as it's coming up, I'll just note that it's a -- this is from the Drina Corps command, from General Krstic, dated 25 September, to, it looks like, most of his brigades, with your brigade on the top of the list, as commander, and to the commanders of those brigades, and it's entitled "Very Urgent." And you'll agree with me that this is the very urgent order for these brigades to gather together parts of their units to go to the Krajina, I believe; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And if we go to the third page in both the B/C/S and the English, we can see that Krstic is ordering that the formation -- down in paragraph 9, that: "All the preparations and formations of units must be completed by 25 September 1995." And then it goes on: "The unit commander and organs of the Brigade Command shall review the troops of the unit and the unit's base garrison between 0700 and 0800 hours, and the units shall set off from their base garrisons towards Kozluk and form marching columns between 0800 and 1000 hours on the 26th of September." So Krstic wants the units formed and marching out of their particular areas by 10.00 a.m., the 26th; correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So when you get back to the Zvornik area on the 25th, you've got a fair amount of work to do?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't do any command-related job on the 26th relating to the Zvornik Brigade. This job was done by Dragan Obrenovic, who stood in for the brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How about Monday, the 25th; what did you do? We can see that you're back in Zvornik. You've acknowledged that.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said in examination-in-chief, what I did when I spoke to Krstic, and that the following day, that is, the 26th, I arrived at the Zvornik Brigade Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So when you spoke to Krstic, as you've described to us, was that the first time you spoke to Krstic that day, the 25th?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, that was our conversation that took place on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, but was that the first time you had spoken to him on the 25th?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As I said, to the best of my recollection, that was our first conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, let's go to -- if we have those two original documents. Just as you recall, General, the first document I want to mention was the one that you talked about in your direct examination, and I believe that is 65 ter 2927. And after you testified about that document, which is, as we know, the Zvornik Brigade version of gearing up a unit to go to the Krajina, we found another document with the same -- which appears to be identical, and I wanted you to have a chance to look at both these originals so you could study them to get a correct and truthful response. The first document that you went over with on direct, you had said that you had signed it on the 26th, when you came to the office; correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And you said that the reason you knew that was because you could tell that you'd signed over the top of the inked, stamped -- the stamp that was on the document; correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because the order of things and the obligations of the Staff office, as such, that signature comes first and then a stamp and comes later. You can never have the other way around.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But which way was it in this case, just to be clear, now that you've seen both these orders?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You, yourself, saw the original. We showed it to Their Honours. And I think you would agree that the stamp was put first, and then over the stamp is my original signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, General. And as I recall, glancing at it, I did agree on the record to that, but I'm sorry. After reviewing both documents now and learning a little bit about ink, I'm going to have to change my mind on that, and I want to see if we can clear this up. After you've had a chance to look at both these originals, and let me give them back to you. And that second one is 2972A and the second one is 2927 -- sorry 2927, not 2972. General, you will agree with me that both those documents are the same document; correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they are identical in substance, but I have to say that the one that I have in my hand, I don't know what exhibit number is that, but I have 0432-7194-2195. That is the original document which has "A/A" at the top, which means that it has been filed in the archives. This document is clearly an original, that the stamp was affixed first and the signature came over the stamp. And we also see that it has been printed by a mechanical printer. However, the other document, if you compare it in terms of the content, we see that the lines do not coincide in both documents. This document was probably stored in a computer, as such, and then printed later on. It does not constitute an original as the one that I described before. At any rate, I am sure and I know that on the 25th September, I was not at the Command HQ, and I didn't address these issues contained in this order. Meanwhile, I remembered one thing, and that is that the gentleman who was in the Staff office had an opportunity to scan my signature. He even did that on one occasion before for certain permits for people, allowing them to cross the border, by scanning it with a computer. All I can assume is that he put stamps on all these documents that he later printed, which he shouldn't have done, and he knew that he couldn't bring them in that condition to me for signing, and therefore he probably scanned my signature and put them on the documents. I am not an expert for this particular area, but I know for sure that I didn't put my signature on this document that bears the date of the 25th [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And so the record is clear, the first document you spoke of that you called the original, that is 65 ter 2927, according to the ERN number that you gave us. All right. General, I won't dwell on this. Let me just tell you the Prosecution's position to see if we can clear it up, and then we'll go on. It's the Prosecution's position, General, that the two documents are identical. You'll agree with me that both documents have original stamps over the signature part; correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they do, and this other document has a black ink signature over the stamp, and it is identical to the signature on the original document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's the Prosecution's position that you signed the original document, and then it was photocopied, and it's the photocopy version that is the second document that you have there, 2927A, and that after you had signed the original, the stamp went on top of the original signature, and then somebody also put an original stamp on the photocopied signature. And if you look carefully at the document, you can see that one is a photocopy of the other, and that's what must have happened.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's your position, which is diametrically opposed to the one that you expressed a few days ago. You had agreed at the time, and you cannot refute that on this first document without the letter E. This is my original signature over the original stamp. If we now look at another document, which also has an original stamp, but the signature is a copy of the original signature from the original document; therefore, the solution that you are proposing is impossible. It is possible to scan the signature from the original document and use it and put it over the stamp in the other document. Whether somebody was abusing something during the war and doing some things that they shouldn't have been doing, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please speak into the microphone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You heard it. Okay, thank you. Yes, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Just before it goes too far, there's a bit of concern about the translation of an answer that Mr. Pandurevic gave on the previous page at lines 20 to 22.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And what is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: He said: "I'm not an expert for this particular area, but I know for sure --" and I'm told he said "but I didn't put my signature on this document on the 25th of September."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you contest that, Mr. McCloskey, or do you want to put it to the witness again?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, I think that's what he's been saying, and I wouldn't think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's why I ask you, because I think I would agree with Mr. Haynes. Okay, let's proceed then. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, General, I don't think it will help us further. We will get a forensic person to look at this for us, which I imagine you wouldn't object to. But you don't have to respond to that without talking to your lawyer, and we'll see how that goes. It's my view that we'll get a forensic person on this before we give it to you, I think, unless you'd like to see this right now. It's whatever you would like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'd like to see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let's just take a moment so you can see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If we could go to 65 ter 2926, and this -- I just is a 25 September Zvornik Brigade regular combat report, and I just want to direct your attention to paragraph 2 to help put us in a time chronology. And if you can blow that section 2 up for you, we'll just see that it -- it says: "At 1500 hours, the Brigade commander, having returned from the Corps where he presented his report, held a meeting with the battalion/artillery battalion commanders and core members of the Command."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And as I recall, it's your position that this is Dragan Obrenovic; correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only is this my position, but Dragan Obrenovic also said that on that day, he was at the corps command, attending a meeting. And you also saw the conversation on the 23rd where Krstic asks Petrovic, "Where is your commander," and he meant Obrenovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, the conversation we saw, it was -- he wanted Vinko to report on Monday morning; right?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he wanted to talk to Vinko. However, on Monday morning, Vinko did not report to the corps command. You also saw the travel log by Dragan Obrenovic which says that he was in Vlasenica on that day. He himself said that he was at that meeting. You also saw the travel logs for my vehicles, and you saw that on the 25th I did not use a single vehicle that I could have used because they were at my disposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, I agree with you that Dragan Obrenovic did go to Vlasenica that day, but let's explore whether or not you went as well. So let's go to 65 ter number 2929. This is an intercept, and go to the one that we've marked on the intercept report. It's page 1 of the English, page 2 of the B/C/S. It's an intercept that begins at 1540 hours, so roughly 40 minutes after a meeting was supposed to have started at the Zvornik Brigade that day. And as we may recall, the English translation has left out that this was between 01 Centrala and Vinko, but that's clear in the original. Now, as we see, it starts out with Vinko saying: "Hello. Put 01 on the line. "One moment." And then 01 gets on the line and says: "Yes. I was resting a bit. "Vinko: I'm sorry. "That's okay. Tell me. "Vinko: Legenda is here with me. "Yes. "We have now defined those tasks and obligations. "Yes. "Now, he is explicit in his demand to act as one. No one should join him, and he does not want to join a larger formation. "Well, okay, let them go as one. "And he would like to use the armoured section. "Yes. "Well, would he be able to for those other reasons? "To do what? "He wants to use his tanks. "His tanks? "Yes. "Well, how is he going to do that? We don't have a freight train, my Vinko. How much fuel would we need to get there? "Well, is that a blitz variant? "Well, it is. No, no, not blitz. "Yes. "Further on. "Yes, ah-hah. "Further on. "Well, I don't know. Then that is a restrictive factor? "Yes. "Just a second, please." So now this is you saying: "Just a second, please," and it appears you're getting off the phone for a moment. You're doing that to talk to someone, I take it. So, is that right, you took a moment to speak to someone in the middle of this conversation?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know there's a break. I did ask for a moment, but I can't remember why as I sit here today.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And as we look at the rest of the conversation, it appears clear that General Krstic is allowing Legenda to take his tank crew but not his tanks; correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And this conversation occurred some 40 minutes after the meeting that the commander was supposed to have at the brigade to talk about important things, and you've told us that this was a conversation you had from a friend's house in Zvornik; correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And if we go to the first page, back to the first page of this conversation, page 2 in the B/C/S, page 1 in the English, right in the beginning you tell General Krstic that: "Legenda is here with me." So is Legenda there with you at your friend's house in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I've already explained why I said what I said. I did it on examination-in-chief. If you look at the conversation, you read "blitz variant," but it's not "blitz," it's a closer and further variant. Those who were typing used two Zs to denote a different sound. You can see from the conversation that I didn't know where Legenda was supposed to go, whether he was supposed to be used. If I had been at the meeting in Vlasenica, I would have known where that unit was being sent, whether it was closer to Banja Luka or further away from Banja Luka. And you can see that I say here: "Is this the closer variant?" Krstic says: "Yes, it's no -- not closer." And then I say: "Yes." And then I said: "Not further, but further away." And then I say: "I understand." So I didn't know what was the plan for Legenda, where was he to be used. If I'd been at the meeting at Vlasenica, then I would have known.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, we see you requesting General Krstic for Legenda to use his tanks, and General Krstic refusing because of fuel, but let me take you back to the first page. After you say: "Legenda is here with me," you say: "We have now defined these tasks and obligations." Those are the tasks and obligations under the Drina Corps order that we just went over; correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I said that I had spoken to Legenda and that this had been said. He told me that everything had been regulated and that he wanted to act in the way as described here. If I had been at this meeting with Krstic in Vlasenica, I'm sure I would have raised those issues up there, and I would have regulated things in advance, and I would have known exactly what would happen with Legenda.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Why would you lie to General Krstic about Legenda being "here" with you? I'm sure General Krstic allows you to go into town briefly from Standard. We've all been there. We all know how close Standard is to town. Why would you have to lie to General Krstic and say, "Legenda is here with me"?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did not allow me to go to town or not allow me. On that day, I was supposed to be with him, but I did not arrive in time. I arrived in Zvornik in the afternoon, and I did not want to go straight to the Command to deal with anything and to disturb the rhythm that was already in place. I reported to Krstic, and that's how I made it clear that I was already at the Command, working. There was no logic in both me and Obrenovic going to the Command HQ to receive our orders. This had never happened. This never happened throughout the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: My question is: Why would you have to lie to General Krstic about this?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not a lie. I simply told him, "Legenda is here with me," which meant, in essence, that I had spoken with Legenda. Legenda was in Zvornik, but he was not standing next to me when I was talking to Krstic. That's -- that was just my way of putting things.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to 65 ter 7D771. This is the trip log that you spoke of. And if we go to the next page of the document in both languages, and if we could blow up the section for 25 September. And could we just put the B/C/S on there. We don't -- and we need the signature side. Right there, perfect. Well, we actually also need the date. Okay. Well, we've just missed the date. Okay, well that will have to be a start. Now, do you remember what you said about this document? I think you said you recognised the signature on the 23rd and 24th, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the 23rd, no, I didn't say that I recognised the signature. And there's no signature on the 24th document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. How about the 25th? Let's blow that -- let's blow that up, if we could, and go over to the signature section, which is right below the blank spot. You testified that on direct that you didn't recognise the name or the signature of that?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is between Zvornik and Belgrade. That was the route. In pencil, the mileage, the number of people, and the number of journeys, and the signature is in ballpoint pen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you can read that as "Danojlovic," can't you?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, one could also read it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So if this is correct, that means Obrenovic's driver went to Belgrade on the 25th?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible he went to Belgrade on the 25th, but there's also another driver, the one who drove Obrenovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And who would that be?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know his name. I saw it in the document that there was another driver who would drive him occasionally. His name may have been Tojic, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's look at another document that was used, 7D772. You can take it out of the package, if you want. And if we could -- we could see that this is only noted for the 20th, the 23rd, the 26th and the 28th. Let's go to the next page to see where it says it's going. And we need the dates on this so we can see. The English cut the dates off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you have only English?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, there's the B/C/S as well, and I think we should try to use the B/C/S. But if we could just. I'm told this was a Defence exhibit, but there's no B/C/S in the record, so I guess we better resurrect ELMO. If we could get the ELMO going, please. Lots of multi-taskings with these things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'm told it's 7D261.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's helpful, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And General, we just note that this is for a vehicle, and the drivers interestingly are Danojlovic and Bogdan Pandurevic, and that we see on the September 25th this vehicle goes to Vlasenica. So isn't this the vehicle that was driven by Bogdan Pandurevic and took you to Vlasenica?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. McCloskey, you're mistaken. You see that the handwriting is the same on the whole page, and this is Ljubisa Danojlovic's handwriting, and you can see that this is Dragan Obrenovic's signature, not mine. And nowhere in this travel log do you see Bogdan Pandurevic's handwriting. He was a possible reserve. That's why his name was recorded here, as a possible reserve driver.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Who is Milutin Tojic?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Milutin Tojic was another driver in the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to 65 ter number 4405, and we do not have an English of this. And at times, Milutin Tojic took Obrenovic around, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since he was a driver at the Command, he was engaged as needed, and he drove the other officers and commanders from the Brigade Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you read that original for us for the date of the 25th? Perhaps we can blow it up on the screen, too. I think we can. As best as you can see, where does it go on the 25th?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says "Zvornik-Vlasenica-Zvornik-Kozluk."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And do you recognise the signature on that date?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm not familiar with the signature, and I see that he made two journeys, and I don't know why. Why would he make two journeys?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, General. Now, we noted in your pre-trial brief, on page 9 and paragraph 26, that you say: "In particular, he asserts that during three significant material periods in the indictment, command of the Zvornik Brigade was de facto and de jure assigned to brigade staff -- sorry, Brigade Chief of Staff Deputy Commander Dragan Obrenovic. These periods were ..." And then on, you say, from 7 August to 16 September, and from 18 September to 24 September. So according to your pre-trial brief, on 25 September Dragan Obrenovic would no longer be the person in command, and is that a mistake, we sometimes make mistakes in our briefs, or is this correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see that this was done in English after consultations with me, and if I had looked at it, I'm sure that I would have noticed the mistake. It says here that on the 3rd of August, I was appointed the commander of the brigade, and as of that day, I started issuing orders and being in command of that brigade. And up to the 16th and including the 16th, I did not take the command over the Zvornik Brigade. On the 17th, I reported to Krstic, I got my days off, and then until the 26th of September I did not take the command over the Zvornik Brigade, which means between the 3rd August and the 26th September.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay, General. So then this is a mistake, as you've said. Let's go to 65 ter number 7D680, and this is a -- I think it's a regular combat report from the Zvornik Brigade. And if my recollection is correct, you have acknowledged you are back in the brigade now and you are in command.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And according to this, there was a team of officers from the Brigade Command analysing operational tasks carried out "last month" and is working on operational task plan for the coming month. And it goes on to say: "The brigade commander held a briefing for artillery battalion commanders, and a command reconnaissance commission is currently underway, led by the brigade commander." And in this report, the brigade commander is you; right?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was after my arrival, and I invited the commanders of the battalions and divisions in order to get an insight into them -- into the overall situation. If I'd been able to do it the previous day, I would have done it, the one day before.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And in your testimony on the 11th of February, page 31242, beginning line 17, you were asked the question by Mr. Haynes: "Now, upon your return to the brigade, did you come to learn about something unusual going on in Zvornik during your absence? "Yes. A few days later, I learned that some trucks had passed through Zvornik and that these trucks were carrying some sort of material which left behind an unbearable stench. I discussed this with Mijo Dragutinovic. He said that probably corpses had been transported and that he knew that the trucks came from the transport company because they had Steyr-make trucks and that the local citizens were upset by that, and this happened in the course of the night." You go on: "I asked him whether the brigade had been assigned any sort of task or issued any sort of order in connection with this, and his answer was, 'No.' He said he had no knowledge and he knew of no details." The Zvornik Brigade was, in fact, involved in that process, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not the Zvornik Brigade, Mr. McCloskey. You cannot say that two men equal the Zvornik Brigade. The Zvornik Brigade was not involved at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Which two men are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The two that I'm referring to are the ones that were mentioned by several witnesses. One of the witnesses was protected, or maybe not, and he said that one piece of machinery was working and that the operator was the person who was involved in the burials, and he was not on the list of the Engineers Company. For this to have been the whole Zvornik Brigade, things should have looked differently. The corps command should have issued an order to the Command of the Zvornik Brigade, and then the Zvornik Brigade would have allocated the resources in the way things would be done, and if several individuals -- two or three people from the Zvornik Brigade are engaged without the knowledge of the Brigade Command, you cannot speak about the participation of the Zvornik Brigade but, rather, about the participation of the two or three individuals in question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You go on to say that you received information that the 5th Engineers was involved as well; correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 5th Engineers Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Right, the folks down in Konjevic Polje, the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This battalion was billeted there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to 65 ter number 1801. This, just as a reminder of what was going on on 27 September, is an aerial image from the United States, dated 27 September, of the Branjevo Farm, with notations from the US. Can we blow that up? Thank you. Can we keep bringing it up a bit. All right. So what we see here, General, is, in the area where the mass grave was originally from the previous photograph we saw from the 17th of July, the United States has noted: "Newly excavated trench." And we see what looks like a shaded area with something piled next to it. And over at the Branjevo farm facilities, we see a blow-up that is identified as: "Backhoe and front loader." So you'll agree with me, sir, that on the 27th, work has clearly begun on picking up the dead bodies and moving them to where we know is on that road to the Cancari village and the Snagovo area; correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't dispute at all that the bodies were removed. However, within which time-frame and the exact dates, I don't know. You are now reading these aerial photographs as if you were an expert. We didn't have any expert coming in here and explaining to us what this is, because there were quite a few agricultural machineries on the farm that might resemble excavator. What you say, that on the left-hand side we can see some excavation, maybe that took place on the 25th, 26th, or even 27th. Affixing these dates, you yourself said was done at a later stage. An aerial photograph must have an automatic inscription of the date when the shot was made. And I have nothing to do with these reburial and transfers regarding these mass graves, irrespective of the dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All I said, General, was that we see this is dated 27th September. There's a large pit that the United States has pointed out to us. We don't need to be an expert. It says: "Newly excavated trench."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I think we can only go so far with this. The United States hasn't come here and pointed out to us anything on these photographs or, indeed, told us what date they were taken on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. But isn't that a submission? I mean ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, this is a submission being made to the witness by Mr. McCloskey, then. If that's what you say to me, then it's equally true of him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, we are fully aware of that, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And I think the question has been answered. Mr. Pandurevic has made every comment he can upon this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Perhaps Mr. Haynes has forgotten, but the United States -- the evidence is the United States stands by the markings in black and white that they have made on these. These are not Mr. Ruez's markings, and that is in the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Again, let's proceed. Basically, don't you agree that he has already answered your question, as such, expressing doubts as to the exact date when the trench could have been excavated, the newly -- new trench?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, and as is the case many times, I agree with the general, and it cannot be determined to be the exact date. All it is, as my question was, is that we see an open trench with heavy equipment close by.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And won't you -- can't you conclude this is ongoing work at this point? This isn't the kind of thing you're going to leave an open trench for for very long?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree perhaps the trench had already been finished, there were no bodies there, the trench needed to be backfilled only. Secondly, according to these photographs, there's only one possible conclusion, and that is that this area was photographed on a daily basis at all time, which I find to be very unlikely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, we don't want to speculate how often the United States was photographing this area, so I don't think we should. Let's go to another exhibit that will help resolve some of this. It's something that's in evidence, has been there for a long time. It's 65 ter number 1868, and this is a close-up aerial image on the same date. And if we could blow that up a little bit more. This is at the site which is known as "Cancari 12," where over 100 human beings were taken out of at an ICTY exhumation, as testified by Mr. Ruez. And you'll agree with me that we see, in this picture, an open pit at the same time we see an open pit at Branjevo Farm? Or the same day, I should say. I won't get into the times since they're not down there.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would kindly ask you to point to me, with your pencil, what you call the pit in this photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You can't see it?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see a lot of things here, but I don't know what particular hole or pit you are referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Re-ask the question. I mean, I would ask you the same question. There are at least three or four items distinguishable on the photo that I wouldn't know what they are, because they haven't got a marking next to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You see the white line that is next to the dark pit right in the center of the photograph. You can see the tracks of the vehicle that went back and forth, back and forth, in digging that?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Well, just for the record, there is 65 ter number 1865 and 186 -- well, let's go to 1865.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. General, let's -- the road on this aerial imagery is the road that goes through the villages in the Snagovo area to the Cancari village. And as we go from right to the left, if you turn left to go towards that house with no roof --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could we blow this up a bit, getting the house and the left turn?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, that is a -- as we turn in towards that house, you can see a darkened area. It doesn't come through quite as well on this, but that is -- does that appear to you to be a pit?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These dark areas look to me like forests.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, I can tell you the evidence in this case will show that it's these -- this particular area in both these photos is where mass graves were exhumed, and many, many people were taken out of this particular area, as it's identified in very particularity on -- in the evidence, and so I'm -- and that is part of the evidence of this case, which I'm sure that if you would compare, you would agree. So if we can conclude that these are open pits on the same day that the pit is open at Branjevo Farm, then on the 27th, during the day, when these photos were taken, the work is not complete yet; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with you concerning the exhumation of the burial sites and their discovery, et cetera, et cetera, only I don't think it's logical to open a primary pit and secondary pits on the same day. I suppose that the secondary pits would have been prepared in advance in order to move the bodies from the primary pit to them. We've seen the village of Cancari, and maybe it would be good if we put these two photographs together on the screen, and let us compare the pits that we saw in the previous photograph and the one that we see here. I do not deny the existence of the pit, but I do deny the time and the dates when they were opened and closed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, let's go to 65 ter 1866, which is a photograph of this very pit that we just looked at, but a few days later, 2 October, and this is earth, showing it to be filled in.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you would agree with me that while we see an open pit on the 27th and we see a closed pit on October 2nd, we don't really know what date between the 27th and October 2nd that it was filled in?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that something was done by the road, but what specifically was done, I don't know. It is interesting how both Branjevo and Cancari were a photographed on the same date, and that is on the 27th September, how the persons taking photographs knew where the secondary pit was going to be. Why don't we have pictures of any other areas that there were no grave -- mass graves in the same period?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, General, Mr. Ruez and Mr. Manning went through all that, but it was a long time ago, so I don't think we need to go over it. Let me now go to the testimony in open session of a member of the Engineering Battalion, Damjan Lazarevic, and you may recall that during his testimony, it was the first time he'd ever mentioned anything about the secondary graves. And on page 14467, by Mr. Thayer, he's asked: "Did you become aware at any time after these events of an operation to dig up all those bodies and rebury them elsewhere? "A. After the initial burial, you mean? "Q. That's correct, sir. "A. I heard about it. "Q. When did you hear about it, sir? "A. After some time. I don't know how much later exactly. "Q. And do you have any information or knowledge about your engineering company being involved in any way in such activities?" The answer that he gave for the first time was: "Yes." And he goes on to say the next page: "I heard that machine operators went somewhere. The ones who did the initial burying were called to dig the bodies out. "Q. And, sir -- I'm sorry, please continue." And he goes on and says: "I was assigned to do that the same way it was done the first time from the engineering base. I was told to go there with them when they began working. They made a list of men. Major Jokic and Slavko Bogicevic did that. They were the people who were supposed to do that." Major Jokic, we know who he is, he is the chief of the engineering company, and Slavko Bogicevic is his deputy, for a better word; correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Jokic was not the chief of the engineering company. He was the chief of engineering, but he spent most of his time with that company. Slavko Bogicevic was assistant for morale and also a deputy company commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you for the correction. Of course, he's chief of Engineering. He goes on to say, page 14484, and Mr. Thayer says: "Now, sir, I just want to ask you some additional questions about the reburial of these bodies. You referred to a list of people that had been compiled and shown to you of people that, I believe, were supposed to work, people that belonged to your company during this operation. Do you know who compiled that list, sir? "A. From my company, two or, rather, three operators were singled out. The rest were from other units, not from the engineering unit. There were only three of our men from our unit. "Q. And when you say 'unit,' sir, are you referring to other units or battalions of the Zvornik Brigade or are you talking about other brigades? "A. I mean other units. From my unit, from the engineering unit, there were only three men. The rest were from the Zvornik Brigade, from its different units." So, so far we have Slavko Bogicevic, Dragan Jokic, Damjan Lazarevic, and the three excavator operators who did the first burial process. And then on page 14485, it says: "Can you describe what kind of vehicles were used in the transport of those bodies? "A. The vehicles of the company, trucks from various companies. Our vehicles were old and we couldn't use them to complete the work." So they're using -- from the Zvornik Brigade, people from the engineering unit are coordinating with private companies because the Zvornik Brigade trucks were not able for the work; is that right? Is that your understanding of what he's saying?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this is not how I understand his words. Obviously, it was someone else who was directing and coordinating this job. I discussed this with Mr. Jokic, and he told me that no one from the engineering company of the Zvornik Brigade was involved in that. After ten years of investigation, you have obtained this information only recently, so this tells us that this was very difficult to discover and find out, particularly at that time. It was impossible for these three men to coordinate this with private companies. This must have done by someone at a much higher level.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General, you know that the information regarding the reburials comes from many different sources, not just this person; correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Perhaps this is a good time for a break. I will definitely finish up by the next session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So, General, you'll agree with me that from Damjan Lazarevic, we know that Dragan Jokic was involved in this process, Bogicevic was involved, three excavator operators were involved, private companies owning the trucks were involved, and from what you, yourself, said, the 5th Engineering was involved, so this would have taken coordination and communication involving significant Zvornik Brigade assets; correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about -- what you said at the end about the assets belonging to the Zvornik Brigade's significant use thereof, I don't know about that. I do agree that we learned about this from Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to 65 ter 379. This is an entry from the duty officer notebook of 27 September. It's just a one-liner, so we'll just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, and I'm sorry to interrupt you, Mr. McCloskey. Mr. Pandurevic, your answer addresses the part of the question allegedly involving significant Zvornik Brigade assets, but doesn't address coordination. If you could answer that part of the question too, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly, Your Honours. I think that the assets of the Zvornik Brigade were not engaged to a great extent. The coordination of all these activities that Mr. McCloskey spoke about was evidently necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And that would have been Dragan Jokic, as the chief of the engineers, as a major coordinator working with, well, at that time you? Obrenovic wasn't around.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have heard from Mr. Lazarevic what Jokic was doing. He said that Jokic didn't coordinate any other activities except for making the list of men. We both agree that these activities had started much earlier, before my return from Montenegro. In other words, the coordination and the engagement of men started in this area much before and without my knowledge. If I had stayed by any chance in Krajina for another month or until the end of the war, these activities would have been completed without my knowledge and participation. These activities definitely started while I was absent and while Dragan Obrenovic was in command of the brigade. I'm not saying that he, himself, was involved in that, because what he told me upon my return from Krajina was that this activity had been organised from the highest level, i.e., from the Main Staff, that it did not have anything to do with the Zvornik Brigade, but rather someone was appointed to coordinate these activities as a chief coordinator and singled out men to do it without -- or actually by bypassing the Zvornik Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you try to speak to Mr. Ovramovic, the commander of the 5th Engineers, on the 25th of September?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember speaking to Mr. Ovramovic in September. I saw him very rarely. Therefore, I cannot tell you anything more with any degree of certainty.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, you've seen the intercept of 27th September, 65 ter number 4293?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've seen it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So do you remember trying to -- we can see that -- we should see it at 65 ter 4293. It seems to be passing on a message from Lieutenant-Colonel Pandurevic to Ovramovic about wanting military policemen. What's this about?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I saw this intercept, I tried to understand what this is all about. Judging by the contents of the conversation, I can establish a link between the engagement of these policemen in that particular period with the activities carried out in terms of controlling the territory because some Serbs came and tried to settle in the abandoned area, and I'm talking about the area of Birac and refugees from Krajina. There were also soldiers who had deserted from the Krajina, and the process of taking them into custody had started. I find it peculiar that someone from the military police is passing on my request to someone else. Therefore, I don't understand why this policeman made this call and why did he speak in this way. This -- if this question had to be resolved, I would directly call the battalion command or the corps command. Otherwise, I really don't understand why they chose to do it this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, General, I agree that the military police would have been partaking in many appropriate tasks, such as you've described. That would be normal. My question is: Why is Major Ovramovic -- why do you need to speak -- why do they need to speak to Major Obramovic -- Ovramovic, excuse me, the commander of the 5th Engineering Unit, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember this conversation or this event. It would be necessary to speak to him, because his unit was involved and he was to accept these men. This is what ensues from this conversation. But if you establish a link between the engagement of these men with something else, then the distance to Konjevic Polje and these places is much longer --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't hear the last part of the last sentence. Apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't hear the last part of the last sentence. If you could repeat it, please, Mr. Pandurevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I was speaking about the fact that if Mr. McCloskey establishes a link between these activities and this conversation with reburials that we discussed earlier, then these sites where the secondary pits were much further from Konjevic Polje than from Zvornik. Therefore, I don't see why these policemen should be deployed in Konjevic Polje and doing some job there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, General, you brought up the 5th Engineers as someone that was reported to you they have been involved in these reburials, and we know from Damjan Lazarevic that his guys were involved in digging up the bodies that they'd originally buried, but he didn't know about what happened to them on the other end. And you have, as I said, suggested the 5th Engineer involvement, so that's why I ask you.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but these can be completely different jobs in which these policemen were involved and the jobs that involved the 5th Engineer Battalion. You see that Lazarevic himself said that where the bodies that were dug up ended. That tells me that at the time, somebody was coordinating this action in such a way that each participant knew only one portion of the operation, starting from the burial site to the site of the subsequent burial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I don't wish to stop this line of cross-examination. I'd just like to know what the Prosecution's position is. This is apparently an intercept between Palma, which we know to be the Zvornik Brigade, and the Customs. Is that accepted to be accurate, or is it now suggested that the participants are other people?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey. Thank you, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: As the questions are clear, I'm asking him. There haven't been really many leading questions. I'm trying to get information from the General, because it says "Lieutenant-Colonel Pandurevic asked you to receive five of his military policemen for five days," and it goes on: "Did Lieutenant-Colonel Pandurevic order that?" And Palma says: "He asked." So the Palma duty officer is saying that Pandurevic is asking something to Ovramovic to do with MPs, and I'm asking him if he remembers. That's as simple as that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Mr. Haynes?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes, but the intercepters of this conversation on which I assume the Prosecution rely, assert that they can identify the participants in the conversation as Palma and Customs, and I just want to know: The Prosecution produced this exhibit, that's what it says, do they assert that this is a conversation between Palma and the Customs?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm trying to find information about this conversation before I decide what it is. I've got a person that's mentioned it here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's proceed, let's proceed. I think it's clear enough. Yes, your next question, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General, under "Participants," it says "Palma" and then what is the Serbian word? Between "Palma" and what?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the second participant?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that this was the secret name for the 5th Engineers Battalion, but I can't be sure of that. I can't really remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Okay. Let's -- and to be clear, I did not remember that. Let's go to --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: To be clear, I didn't even know it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think we're getting near the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go back. I think we were at the duty officer notebook of 27 September, and this is a one-liner. If we could -- it's 65 ter 379. B/C/S, page 140; English, 140. And it's the segment between 1113 hours and 1925 hours that I want you to look at, so if we could go down a little bit on the B/C/S. There we go. I'm sure you've read this, and you were the commander at that point, and it says: "Remind the commander about the construction work." Now, I'm sure you read this and you thought about it. Do you remember what construction work you would have been reminded of?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's about construction workers, the handymen who were repairing things. So it's not about constructions or construction work, but construction workers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, what about them?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were people who were working in the HQ Administration, in the Logistics, repairing facilities. They had to be engaged somewhere. At the time, there was a course attended by company commanders. The accommodation had to be provided for them. Things had to be repaired, put in good working order, so I suppose they were engaged on such things.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So somebody reminded you about looking after some construction workers for some construction project in the HQ?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For some construction works, whether in the Command or in a facility -- or some other facility. I know that the course for the company commanders had been underway in the youth camp. That's where they were accommodated. I suppose that some facilities needed to be repaired there, or something to that effect. I really don't know. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to 65 ter 4299. This is also dated 27 September, from the Zvornik Brigade, signed, I believe, by you. If you could confirm that for us.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And it's a longer document than some we've seen, so it's -- it's entitled "Report on the state of morale for September 1995. Submission." And then it says: "Short description of the activities of the brigade in the last period." And I really only want to ask you about two things. It's page 4 of the English, page 2 of the B/C/S, and it's right at the bottom, maybe the bottom of page 1 of the B/C/S. It's under the B/C/S section for negative morale factors, and it's the last negative morale factor. It's page 4, if we could bring the English down a little bit. It's probably down at the bottom of page 1 of the B/C/S, and it's on page 4 of the English. Let's try page 2 of the B/C/S, and could we go up with the English to get that last -- that sentence, it's just. There you go. So this factor, it says: "The worn-down condition of quartermaster supplies, especially clothing and footwear of the majority of the soldiers, which will make life and work of the units significantly more difficult in the upcoming winter conditions, and the insecurity of a quick resolution of the issue." So were your uniforms and your boots in bad repair, like this says?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, nothing new. It was that way throughout the war. We always had that problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now let's go to "Positive Morale Factors." And looking at the second paragraph under the positive morale factors section, it says: "A high level of trust in the Brigade among the commanding staff, the soldiers, and amongst each other, which is constantly increased with the process of building a military organisation and the direct presence of members of the Command at the units." Do you stand by that?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this was one of the positive factors that had a positive impact on morale. Maybe it was not to that particular degree, the high degree of confidence in the brigade. However, if that is high, it has a high impact. My assistant for morale had to highlight certain positive factors. In any case, a certain degree of confidence did exist. If that confidence had not exited, we would not have been able to function.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you signed off on this document firmly believing in what was said in that paragraph at the time?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I signed it. I'm sure I did not read it. But if you look at the October document, which analyses the participation of the Drina Brigade in the fighting in Krajina, you will see things described in a different way. I was the one who had compiled that report, and I highlighted the organisational problems and the problems of command in the Army of Republika Srpska, and I also said that the level of those was not as high as is described in this report that we're looking at. We should have only been so lucky to have things this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you read this or not - it was a little unclear from the interpretation - before signing it?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that I read the entire document, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General, you just don't seem like the kind of general that signs your name without reading a document that's going out to your people or your superiors. You're saying you didn't read all this, huh?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, the assistant commanders are responsible for their own work to the commander, and the state of morale is within the purview of the assistant commander for morale. The commander is responsible for all the elements of combat preparedness. This is a standard monthly report on the state of morale, and if we were to compare this one with the reports for any of the previous months, you would not see a major difference. Unless there had been some drastic changes on the front-lines, this would have been reflected in a report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, let's go on, General, but try to listen to my question and we'll get through here. Now I want to take you -- if we could go into private session briefly, and I'll try to remember to get out of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Let's go into private session for a short while.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. All right, and if we could go to 65 ter number 389.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General, this -- I'm not going to get into the details. This is the statement the military police took. You'll remember the testimony of the military police officer, and this is the person named Sakib Kiviric, age 31, from the village of Jagonje. And as we -- if we went through the other statements, 65 ter 390, we would have Emin Mustafavic, age 25, providing a similar statement; Fuad Dosic, age 30, providing a similar statement; that's 65 ter 399. And we can see from these statements there is no discussion of surviving a mass execution, which I'm sure you notice from the statements, but that in these statements they describe getting helped by a Serb farmer and his son, and they give them clothes, they give them some food, and they point them in the direction of Teocak. And after these Muslims -- four Muslims get arrested, they tell the military police or they tell their captors this story, and these statements are taken by the military police pursuant to a prosecution of this farmer and his son for aiding the enemy. And this is documented by the military police, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And let's go to 65 ter number 392. This is the statement of Almir Halilovic, son of Suljo and Dika, born 25 August 1980 in the village of Bajramovici in Srebrenica. So Almir at the time is a 14-year-old boy; right?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 25th August 1980, so he would be 15 in a month's time at the time. He was a minor, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: He was 14 at the time, right, General?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to 65 ter number 343. This is a statement taken by the military police, the military post of Zvornik, the Crime Prevention Service. And I don't want to spend a lot of time on this, but this is the interview of the father, the man that helped this boy and his three adult companions, and he says, in the first paragraph, this is: "On 18 July 1995, I got up early in the morning to bring grass for my cattle from a field which is about 150 metres from the house." So 18 July, we know, would be two days after the executions at Branjevo were finished, because they finished the evening of 16 July. And he goes on to say: "I knew immediately that they were Muslims, since they were covered with blood, and also by their clothes, because they had been fleeing from Srebrenica towards their territory at that time." So the fact that they were covered with blood two days after crawling out from underneath a mass execution is a pretty good indication, along with their location, that they are from Branjevo Farm, one of them being from the same village as a guy that Amo Hasic remembers; correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, yes, this is what the statement says.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And in the end, Mr. Djokic says: "My son probably did not report them because he was afraid for me, since I had not reported them. I still don't understand why I did not do so. Money cannot be the reason, since they did not have any. I wanted to inform my son about their presence, and in the end everything came out the worst." This is a Serb farmer looking after a Muslim neighbour that needed food and clothing, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they tried to help them and provide protection for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And let's go to 65 ter 385. This is a document indicating a "Ruling," against the father and the son, providing for detention, providing the reasons, in the name of Chief of Security Drago Nikolic. You would have had to approve any punishment of your soldiers for assisting Muslims like this, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean by I would have had to confirm the punishment of my soldiers. The security organ, acting ex officio and in compliance with their obligations according to the rules, estimated that this constituted cooperation with the enemy and punished these two men by imposing three days of -- in detention, and then submitted a criminal charge to the prosecutors. This did not require any authorisations either from the commander or from someone else. I don't remember at all punishing anyone for cooperating with the enemy. If there is any such order, I would really like to see it, but I don't remember doing any such thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But you would have, as the commander, have to know and approve any punishment of your troops. Certainly, you're not suggesting Second Lieutenant Drago Nikolic can, on his own, punish your troops.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If there's a provision in the law allowing him to do this, he doesn't need my consent. If he's entitled to put somebody in custody for three days or 72 hours, he doesn't need my consent. If a battalion commander can punish a soldier by a term of imprisonment or detention, seven days or fourteen days, it's his right, it's his legal right. I never saw this ruling before. As I can see from this material, this criminal charge was rejected by the prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you have no knowledge whatsoever of this investigation, the conclusions, the results, the punishment, and if anyone does, it's only little Drago Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I can conclude from all this is that the whole proceedings were conducted by Drago Nikolic. He was the one issuing the rulings. He took the statement. We see that the four gave almost identical statements, that they were apparently or obviously dictated, and that they signed them as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. General, one last question, and I want to ask you about the brief statement a witness said in this case, and he said it, in particular, in the Krstic case, a statement I'll never forget. I want to read it to you and ask you if you agree with it. The Judges in the Krstic case asked him, and this was the -- he testified in this case as PW-113, a survivor of the Petkovski Dam, one of the two that helped each other survive, and it's a young guy, a young Muslim man. You may remember him. He was the one that remembered seeing his teacher right as he was getting off the truck. And when the Judge asked him if he had anything else to say, he said this: "From all of whatever I have said and what I saw, I could come to the conclusion that this was extremely well organised. It was systematic killing and that the organisers of that do not deserve to be at liberty. And if I had the right and courage, in the name of all those innocents and all those victims, I would forgive the actual perpetrators of the executions because they were misled." That's all. Were the actual -- do you agree with him? Were the actual perpetrators of this, the shooters, were they misled?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I fully understand. I have compassion for the victims. It is very difficult for me to talk about them. I agree, however, what -- with what this gentleman said. This couldn't have been done without proper organisation. Whether that was organised at a higher level, I don't know, because I don't have any authentic information about this. Those who participated in the executions themselves, whether they were misled or not, I believe that some individuals did it consciously because that was in their nature. But at any rate, that was a wrong approach, it was a wrong step, and it sowed poison in this area that is for many years to come help wheat grow among the Serbian people, and this is more harmful and this is a bigger crime than anything else that could have happened there. As much as the people who were executed for -- victims, so are the people who live in the area are victims, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let me, in response to that, you said on page 31962, in response to Mr. Ostojic: "Let me interpret that for you. Drago Nikolic was duty-bound to act upon Popovic -- Popovic and Beara's orders, and they were not from the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, and they did not ask for any man to be taken from some way. They just asked for assistance to carry out the job that was given to them, the job that they were given to do." I think we'll agree that Drago Nikolic was given the job to detain and organise the detention, the transportation, and the execution. Are you standing by this, that he was duty-bound to do that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: He's putting to him Mr. Ostojic's words and asking him if he stands by Mr. Ostojic's words. That's not a fair question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Those aren't Mr. Ostojic's words. I can read the whole thing, if you'd like. That's his answer: "So tell me this --" This is Ostojic: "So tell me this. Can someone from the corps, a colonel or a general from the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, come into the Zvornik Brigade and move a battalion, a platoon, a unit, or even a soldier and say, 'Well, come out of the Zvornik Brigade and come and do this for me, like help me on the front-line, where I'm fighting near Sarajevo'? Do you think that's prescribed by the rules anywhere, sir?" Your answer: "It is prescribed, but let's not go all the way to Sarajevo. There are events that took place closer. If that was needed by Sarajevo Romanija Corps, you would have asked for that from the Main Staff and then the order would arrive at the Drina Corps and then at the brigade. We had a very specific situation in which people came from the Corps and the Main Staff with an order probably issued by the commander of the Main Staff, and they got in touch by the functional line of work with the people of the Zvornik Brigade, and that functional relationship became the relationship that's binding on both parties upon the request of the people from the Corps and the Main Staff." You go on: "Let me interpret that for you. Drago Nikolic was duty-bound to act upon Popovic -- Popovic and Beara's orders." And my question is: As you'll agree, Drago Nikolic was assigned this awful task. Are you standing by this and saying that he was duty-bound to follow it, or do you want to change your testimony?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not changing my testimony. I stand by what I said, that it was his duty to carry out the orders of Mr. Popovic and Beara. What Obrenovic told him was no indication or not indicative at all that he was going to carry out the task of execution. If he carried out this task, he would have done that on the orders of these two men.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General, you were talking about the murder operation, and you said he was duty-bound?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was his duty to obey their orders. If he carried out illegal orders and which constitute serious crimes, then he knew how to act in this situation. If he acted upon their orders and took part in the killing, then he did so. If he didn't, he didn't. If he followed their orders, he committed a crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you'll agree with me that Drago, Popovic, anyone, yourself, but anyone that received an order to take part in this murder operation was duty-bound not to follow it; correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. So -- and that was under the JNA, the VRS, the Geneva Conventions, correct, which you knew?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So if someone, despite their duty not to carry out an order to take part in this operation, took part in the operation, they would have done so on their own free will, against their duty; correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. We have been construing rules here the whole time. Had everybody stuck to the rules, there wouldn't have been any crime. There is no rule prescribing how to commit a crime, but rather rules that say how not to commit a crime and how to prevent it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But my point is: When you walk away from your duty, you do it voluntarily?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure if I understand you correctly, if we do not fulfill our duty, that we do it voluntarily. Can you please be more specific?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: When Drago or you, or anyone that's ordered to commit a heinous crime, knowing it's their duty not to do it, in fact does it, they are doing it voluntarily, no one's putting a gun to their head?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, nobody was putting a gun to their head. Somebody had given them these tasks. They carried out these tasks. THE INTERPRETERS: Witness please repeat whether he said "they were aware" or "weren't aware" of committing the crime.
