utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The interpreters would like to know whether you said that they were aware or were not aware of committing a crime.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were aware.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Bourgon. I'm also coming to you, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, perhaps I can start. With 20 -- well, a little under 20 minutes to the next break, I had been alerted by Mr. Josse that there's something he wants to raise before I start. I see now Mr. Bourgon is rising. I'd like a little time to set up, so can we deal with these procedural matters and then take the next break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. I saw you first, Mr. Bourgon. I haven't seen Mr. Josse indicating that he wants to intervene as well. You do, I assume.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, what I'm interested in is totally unrelated to the evidence of this witness, but I would quite like to deal with it in a few minutes' time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's hear Mr. Bourgon first.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Good morning Judges. Mr. President, at the beginning of the testimony of this witness or at the beginning of the cross-examination, upon our request for the Prosecution to go first which was denied by the Trial Chamber we were informed that should any matter new be brought up during the cross-examination by the Prosecution that we could seek leave of the Trial Chamber to address these issues in further cross-examination. Four such issues have arisen today which I would like to address in further cross-examination. And, Mr. President, I draw your attention to page 3 of the transcript today, at lines 15 and 16, about the identity of the duty officer as something entirely new that was raised today. On page 41, lines 16 to 20, and on the same issue, page 49, lines 7 to 16, in relation to document 65 ter 385, whether the proceedings were instituted by Drago Nikolic alone and whether those charges against the two members of the Zvornik Brigade, where they apparently assisted the enemy, were brought by Drago Nikolic. And finally, Mr. President, the other issue is the one that was just raised by my colleague from the Prosecution at page 52, lines 9 to 25, and page 53. So it's actually three issues that I'd like to briefly address in cross-examination, but I do require some time to speak with Mr. Nikolic before I do so, especially the part with page 41 and page 49. There is one question I need to discuss with Mr. Nikolic before I do this additional cross-examination. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bourgon. Mr. Josse, do you wish -- well, let's hear what Mr. Josse has to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It is unrelated. Do you wish to comment on -- and I will ask you, Mr. Haynes, as well on Mr. Bourgon's --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yeah, I do not object to 2 and 3. 1 has been an issue that was clearly part of the testimony, but it's a short issue, so as long as we don't take forever on it, I won't object to that, either. It's something that came up in direct, and it was -- kind of left a very obvious question to be asked. As you'll recall, he describes going up the stairs and seeing the duty officer, but never names them. So -- but it's a short issue. I don't have -- as long as we don't go on forever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, I do object. The first issue is plain on the face of the Zvornik Brigade records and is capable of stipulation. The second is in the indictment and has previously been heavily litigated, amongst other people, with a witness called Nebojsa Jeremic, and the third is a matter of trite law. They could all have been well anticipated as being matters that should have been dealt with in cross-examination the first time 'round. The witness has been giving evidence now for a very long time. He's looking very tired, if I may say so, and there's no need to deal with these matters now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you wish to reply to that, Mr. Bourgon?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Indeed, Mr. President. These issues were not raised during examination-in-chief, and they were not -- they were raised for the first time during cross-examination of the Prosecution, which is conducted after the cross-examination which was conducted by all Defence teams. And I need very little time to address all of these issues, no more than ten minutes to cover all issues, after I speak with Mr. Nikolic. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. You will soon hear our decision on that. Mr. Josse, on a completely unrelated matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes. Two matters which are related to each other, but are completely unrelated to the evidence of the present witness. The Defence, Your Honours, are aware of a decision of the Appeals Chamber in the Prlic case, dated the 26th of February of this year, that may have some impact on the two outstanding objection motions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour's clearly aware of that. You're also aware that filings are complete so far as those various objections are concerned. Really, we wanted guidance as to whether the Trial Chamber wanted any further submission from any interested party on that particular topic. I'm not inviting the Trial Chamber to allow further submissions, but if you do, could you indicate that they all be filed on the same day by any interested party, rather than having a ping-pong situation of one party putting in a submission and then another. The decision clearly impacts on the issue, and also the Trial Chamber's guidance of the 17th of December of last year, so we are, on behalf of General Gvero, quite content to leave it to the Trial Chamber to indicate whether further submissions are required. The second related issue is this, and I'm just going to read this out verbatim. Following discussions between the Prosecution and the Gvero team, the Gvero team wish to make it clear that they are not objecting, or we are not objecting, to the admission into evidence of P4208. In those circumstances, the Prosecution are not pursuing their application to have P4220 admitted. The Trial Chamber can refer back to what all that relates to, but it's basically matters that came out of Mr. Kosovac' testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I'll start with you, Mr. Josse, in relation to the first issue you raised. Okay, you can remain -- you may remain seated. As you can imagine, I mean, the Appeals Chamber decision in Prlic is something that we went through very careful, and I'm grateful for you -- grateful to you for having raised the issue, and I can confirm to you that we don't need any further submissions from any of you on that matter. In relation to your second submission, those two documents, I think we need to digest it a little bit further. As regards your request, Mr. Bourgon, for a further cross-examination, we are granting your request. We suggest to you to dedicate very little time on the first one, because I think much of the submissions made are very valid. Ultimately, you can refer to the witness's answer this morning, which doesn't add much to what we already knew. We are going to have the break now, and I want to make sure that the security people make it possible for Mr. Bourgon to have consultations with his client.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Of course, you will need to stick to your promise to keep your cross-examination limited to ten minutes. We'll have a 25 minutes' break from now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So Mr. Bourgon, it's 12.30.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Further cross-examination by Mr. Bourgon:

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I have some further questions for you this morning, further to the cross-examination conducted by my colleague from the Prosecution. The first one relates to an answer you gave on page 3, lines 15 to 16. Of course, I just say the page number to allow my colleagues to follow. And you mentioned on that moment, and I quote: "It's correct that they do not resemble each other." And that's because the Prosecutor was asking you to make a parallel between Jokic and Drago Nikolic. And you went on to say: "For a time Mr. Simic, or at least he was supposed to be on duty that day, but for some reasons he couldn't, but it could have been Mr. Nikolic then." My question is the following: Is the first time that you name of Simic is mentioned by yourself throughout your testimony, I'd just like to confirm with this was not information that you had at the time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And on the 15th of July, correct me if I'm wrong, but it would have been normal for Mr. Simic, being the assistant commander for morale and religious affairs, to be quite busy on that day because of the number of people killed from the Zvornik Brigade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was also doing that, but on the 15th there were no major losses. He was involved in something that concerned burials as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: When you say "burials," what burials are you referring to? You're talking about members of the Zvornik Brigade who were killed in action; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The second issue that I'd like to address was raised by yourself or by the Prosecution at page 41, lines 16 to 20, and then again page 49, lines 7 to 16. If I can have in e-court, please, P385. Sir, this is a document that was shown to you by the Prosecution, and it was your testimony that you were not made aware of this document at the time. Now, my first question is the following: Can you confirm that this is not any type of judgement or punishment, but that it is nothing more than detention being ordered by the security organ while the matter is being assessed by the security organ; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a decision that was issued by the security organ. When it came to crimes within the jurisdiction of military courts, this is done ex officio. The person that committed a crime may be kept in custody for up to three days, and later that person's destiny is decided by the military prosecutor. And it says in the rules of the security services that this custody is within the jurisdiction of the security organs at the army level. Whether Drago had the right to do it by law or not, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But you can confirm that this is not a punishment; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this is part of the investigation stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you have seen, at some point in this case, the criminal report that was filed by Drago Nikolic concerning the father and son Djokic; you recall that?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I saw those documents together with the rest of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And my last question on this topic is the following: The Prosecution -- maybe we need to go into closed session -- private session, Mr. President, for a few seconds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's do that. Let's go into private session for a short while, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, on page 52 and 53, my colleague raised with you a long hypothetical with "if there was an order," and "if they abide by the order" or "if they refuse the order." My question is not so much related to the hypothetical itself, but rather to the following: During the period 18 July 1995, when you sent your interim combat report to the corps, first I'd like to confirm that you know which combat report I'm talking about. Do you recall your combat report that you sent on the 18th of July?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, between the moment when you send that interim combat report on 18 July and the meeting you had with all the brigade commanders, as well as your assistant commander, on 23 July, can you confirm that at no point you met with Drago Nikolic to discuss any type of involvement he would have had in the activities which you had learned by 18 July?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. No further questions. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bourgon. Mr. Haynes, I take it you won't finish today now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Sadly, no, but I was going to commence, actually, by telling everybody the good news. I'm pretty precise with these things, and I think I have an hour and a half to two hours re-examination, no more. So I will take the rest of today and no more than one session tomorrow. I've let everybody know this privately, because they've all inquired, and that is that having seen the cross-examination of my client and what has been put to him and, more particularly, what has not been put to him, we have already taken a pretty bold view of the remainder of our case, and granted your very kind break starting tomorrow, we will commence to call evidence next Monday. But I think I can say now it will not occupy a week of the Court's time, and it may only involve the Court sitting on one or two days next week. Now, everybody knows that, and when Mr. Pandurevic and I have had a day's rest, we will confirm that in writing to everybody, but I let you know that and I let everybody else know that so that we can programme for the future. So I'll say no more now, unless anybody else wants to comment before I start asking questions, but those who want to call further evidence better start making preparations to do so next week, unless we're to have another hiatus.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. McCloskey, are you still expecting to file your motion for rebuttal by today?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right, okay, thank you. So, Mr. Haynes, take your time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I just want to start, Mr. Pandurevic, by tidying up a day about which you've been asked quite a lot of questions, and that is the 25th of September. And I think we need to start by looking at P67 -- sorry, 7D679, the regular combat report for the 25th of September.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: P2926 is the same thing?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'll take your word for it, Judge Kwon. You're almost certainly right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: We see there a reference to a meeting or an event at 1500 hours. What does it apparently describe?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In paragraph 2, it says that at 1500 hours, the brigade commander, having returned from the corps where he presented his report, held a meeting with the battalion -- artillery battalion commanders and the core members of the command. This means that in the course of that day, Obrenovic, who had attended a meeting in Vlasenica and received his orders there, with regard to the engagement of the units in the area of the 1st Krajina Corps, called battalion commanders and the core members of the Command and regulated all the issues that arose from the orders given to him by General Krstic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Presumably, at some stage you've held a meeting like that, have you, as commander?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And how long would a meeting like that take?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this case, when you had battalion commanders, artillery battalion commanders, and inner command, the meetings are not short. They last anything above one hour, one and a half hours, sometimes even longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now can we have a look, please, at P379, the duty operations officer's log-book for the month of September, amongst other things, page 137 in e-court, that is. Now, the English, of course, is typed and far more easy to understand, but can you find an entry that relates to the time 1515 or quarter past 3.00 in the afternoon?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see an entry at 1500 hours, being in the ops room, a telegram sent at 1300, if that's what you had in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: The entry I had in mind refers to Velika Pecina, which I think means "caves," doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see the whole page. Maybe that is towards the end of the page. I really can't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think I see it there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: It's about a third of the way down, you can see on the right -- towards the right-hand side of the page "1515." Can you see it. Well, I'll read the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Two lines above the number which is written, reversely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The cursor is pointing to the relevant line, if you look at the right-hand --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can now see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And what does that say in the original so that we can check that the translation is accurate?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Observing at Velika Pecina at 1515, from the Ramici sector ...," and then I can't read the next word, "... from the direction of Sapna, four buses."

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Okay. Now, that's quarter past 3.00 in the afternoon. Can we go down a little further to the entry one line from the bottom, and it's a number.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "584-726 Commander."

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And whose number is that?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the number that was mentioned in the directory from which I would phone in, and that's the number of my friends in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And where were you in the mid to late afternoon of the 25th of September?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spent some time with the friend, and then I went to the house in Celopek to spend some time with the lady with whom I was involved at the time and where I spent time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And who provided that number to be entered in the duty operations officer's log-book?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was the one who provided them with the number where they can call me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, we'll leave that topic now. Something completely different, Mr. Pandurevic. Do you remember when I first became your counsel?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: When was it?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In February 2006, that's when we met for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And have you got any idea how many hours we've spent together since then?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's very hard for me to give you any numbers, but I can say that it was hours and hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And just for all of our benefits: Do we discuss together topics to be asked of witnesses who come to give evidence in the case?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we have discussed that as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Do you write the questions I ask of witnesses?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the questions that you put to the witnesses, I've never written them down, but they differed quite a lot from what I considered to be important to put to the witnesses when they come to the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: You've probably already, therefore, answered this next question, which is: Does everything we discuss end up being put to a witness as a question?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, our discussions are much longer. We discuss a lot more issues and facts, and much less is being presented by yourself in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And what about your own evidence before this Court? Were there things that we discussed in preparation that you haven't told us about?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: You write your own filings and submissions for presentation to the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I've never written a single submission for the Trial Chamber. I have still not advanced that far.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: In particular, did --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Mr. Bourgon, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. It's not -- I would like to avoid interrupting my colleague. However, during cross-examination of Mr. Pandurevic we made a point, and it was even brought quite forcefully to my attention by my colleague from the Prosecution, not to enter into the area of solicitor-client privilege. Now, I have a feeling that what my colleague is doing now is that he is kind of waiving the solicitor-client privilege by entering into discussions and entering into what was discussed between him and his client. Should that be the case, Mr. President, this opens up a whole new area of cross-examination, which may of course call us to ask for further cross-examination to enter into those discussions, and to examine those, and to cross-examine what happened between, you know, my colleague and his client, if he's waiving that privilege, because that's what he's doing with the kind of questions he's putting. I waited until I was confident that this was the case, and I am now confident that this is the case, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bourgon. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm starting to have similar concerns. But if it's just to the area that I brought up about the filing regarding the 25th of September, and it ends there, I think we're okay, and that seems to me where he's going. But much further, and it is getting into an area that, frankly, is an area that we're not used to going into, and I don't think -- we've got to be careful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I agree with Mr. Bourgon, and I think he not only kind of waives the attorney-client privilege, I think he actually does waive it with this line of questioning. We were prohibiting from going into these discussions because they raised an issue of attorney-client privilege, which we respected. Now he wants to come through the back door when he wouldn't allow us to ask through the front door, which is inappropriate. And certainly if he's going to ask these questions, we would have leave to ask further questions of Mr. Pandurevic on these issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Haynes. Thank you, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I didn't stop them. I let them --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You couldn't, either.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: No. I let them ask questions about Mr. Pandurevic's instructions to me and whether they were reflected in his Rule 65 ter summary, whether they were reflected in his pre-trial brief, whether they were reflected in the cross-examination of PW-168, and so this is a classic example of an issue in re-examination arising directly from the cross-examination, and I'm perfectly entitled to establish whether any, on the face of it, deficiencies in those documents are attributable to Mr. Pandurevic or are attributable to his lawyer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So I've had consultations with my colleagues, and the unanimous position here is that there is absolutely nothing irregular going on. And provided this is limited to what Mr. Haynes has just stated, we see no grounds for any further cross-examinations. So let's proceed and conclude on this part, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'll be as quick as I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did you write the 65 ter summary of your evidence or the evidence of any other witness on your witness list?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did you compose the cross-examination of PW-168?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, within the scope of the possible examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did you feel that the cross-examination of PW-168 had covered all the ground you wanted it to?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not in the least.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Was it your decision that it shouldn't cover all the ground you wanted it to?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it wasn't, it wasn't my decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: How did you feel about that at the time?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not entirely happy with the whole thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: What, in particular, were you unhappy about?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In particular, because there was some areas that I wanted the witness to be questioned, and at some points you were interrupted by the Honourable Trial Chamber disallowing you to explore those matters any further.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Was it your decision not to include details of the conversation with Dragan Obrenovic on the 16th of July in your 65 ter summary of your evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Same objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I don't think we need to hear submissions. Let's proceed. Can you answer the question, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. My answer is, "No."

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Was it your decision not to include reference to the involvement of the security organ in the bringing of prisoners to Zvornik in your 65 ter summary?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Or the meeting with Dragan Obrenovic on the 23rd of July?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Or the meeting with General Krstic on the 27th of July?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: When did you first notice those omissions in your Rule 65 ter summary?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw some when the dead-line expired for the submission of the 65 ter submission, so I was shown the final version, the one that was then submitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did you tell Eileen Gilleece about the meeting with Dragan Obrenovic on the 16th of July?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not about the details. I just told her when he informed me about the presence of prisoners in the area of Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did you tell your own lawyers about it?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did. I told them everything I knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: When did you first tell them about it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, we are definitely getting into solicitor-client privilege issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The solicitor-client privilege is none of your concern, Mr. Bourgon. It only becomes your concern when you try to violate it, and then you are stopped. Otherwise, it's a subject matter of relationship between client and counsel, and counsel can deal with this matter provided his client does not object to it. Otherwise, please sit down, both of you, and let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'd like to address the Court, I'd like to address this Trial Chamber. I'm not saying that it's a violation. I'm just saying that he is waiving the privilege, and then I will be asking for further cross-examination on the basis that the privilege has been waived. The rule --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. You can ask later on, and then we will decide.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you for your patience, Mr. President. We also would just like to be -- put the Court on notice. We are inviting Mr. Haynes and Mr. Sarapa to testify, based on this incredible evidence that we are hearing now, although they could have amended 65 ter lists and other things, but we're just putting them on notice if they're entering into this discussion. The only person who could possibly even remotely corroborate any of this would be their very own counsel, and we will be asking the Court for leave to do that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Please do. Yes, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Would you answer the question, please, Mr. Pandurevic, which was: When did you first tell your lawyers about the meeting on the 16th of July?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know it was a long time ago. We analysed facts and events, and that must have been over too long -- two years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, you're not a lawyer, but what was your understanding of the purpose of preparing Rule 65 ter summaries?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understood the Rule this way: I believed that it was a way to submit documents from which the Prosecutor and the Honourable Chamber would see what the Defence case was, what witnesses would be brought, and the principal facts that they would testify about, in order for everybody to be prepared and to be able to prepare for their work.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And have you read many 65 ter summaries in this case?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have read the 65 ter summaries of all the co-accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And how enlightening have you found them to be?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was some submissions, but only two or three main points outlined in them, and no inferences could be made based on those.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Any particular criticisms you've got to make?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't want to make any criticisms. I only remember Mr. Beara's submission, in which he mentioned some witnesses only by their initials or by their names, and I never knew what they would be testifying about.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now let's move on. You told us, when you were being cross-examined by Mr. Bourgon, that in 2005 you sat down to talk to Mr. Bourgon and Ms. Nikolic. What was your motivation for doing that?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They expressed a desire to talk to me. I accepted that. I did not know what they wanted to hear from me, but there was no reason for me to refuse that meeting with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did you do so happily and willingly?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did willingly, of my own will, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And were you content that notes of your conversation should be kept by Drago Nikolic's lawyers?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was at the very beginning, when I was still not very familiar with the Rules of Evidence, and I didn't know whether they were supposed to take notes or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can you recall whether at that stage you had already decided that you would give evidence in your own defence?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: That's an ambiguous answer. Do you mean, yes, you had decided or, yes, you recall?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had already decided to testify in my own case before that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: This may not be clear from your previous answers, but were you aware that notes were being taken by Drago Nikolic's lawyers of your conversation?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. They had papers on the desk. They put some questions. Whether they made notes and, if they did, what notes those were, I really can't tell you with any degree of certainty.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Were you ever shown any note?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did you give an interview to the lawyers for any of the other accused on this indictment?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Was that because you weren't asked or because of some special relationship with Drago Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no special relationship. Nobody explicitly asked for an interview, and when I applied to testify, nobody expressed an explicit desire to talk to me; hence, I haven't spoken to any other Defence team.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we go into private session now, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are whack in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Just remind us what it was that Drago Nikolic told you about the involve -- sorry, that Dragan Obrenovic told you about the involvement of Drago Nikolic in the events of 13th to 16th of July.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He told me that on the 13th, Drago conveyed a message to him that a certain number of prisoners would arrive in the territory of Zvornik, that they should be accommodated there, that a triage should be carried out, and that the rest should be sent to either the Batkovici camp or to be exchanged, that they should be escorted and secured, and that he required a few policemen for that purpose, because he was supposed to wait for the column with prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Was it your intention, in giving evidence in your defence, to cause any additional problems for Drago Nikolic that were not already disclosed by the evidence in this case?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think that I have added any -- anything new that has not already been heard in evidence in this case about any of my co-accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: What did you understand Mr. Bourgon to mean when he said to you, as he did on several occasions to preface a question, "I'm putting this to you because of the way you testified against Drago Nikolic"?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have not testified against anybody in this case. I have just spoken about the facts that I know, and I've only answered questions. I believe that it is my duty. I have taken an oath to tell the truth, and I believe that this is my duty. How the facts are related to each of the co-accused and how each of them experienced and perceived the way the facts are being described, that's their personal matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, I want to see if you understand what was put to you by, in particular, Mr. Bourgon and Mr. Ostojic. Did you understand that it was being suggested to you that you had lied on oath?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I just waited until the answer was on the record for this last answer. I'd like to refer the Trial Chamber to page 78, line 19 and 20, where my colleague said: "What did you understand Mr. Bourgon, when he said to you, as he did on several occasions to preface a question, 'I'm putting this to you because of the way you testified against Drago Nikolic.'" I don't recall I used the word "against" Drago Nikolic, but I used the word "concerning" Drago Nikolic. Unless my colleague can provide me with a reference. I've just checked two of those references and twice I had the word "concerning," on the record, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Accepted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Accepted. I am pretty sure you are right, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'm pretty sure he is, too. I've got all the references here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did you also understand that Mr. Bourgon was suggesting to you that you had conspired together with Dragan Obrenovic to tell lies or pervert the course of justice in a conversation in 1999 or 2000?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's how I understood it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And did you understand that Mr. Ostojic was suggesting to you that you had copied the failed Defence of General Krstic?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But if I had copied something that failed, that would have made me a lunatic, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: When did you first learn that General Krstic had received a sentence of 43 years imprisonment?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the sentence was handed down.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Was that before or after you spoke to Eileen Gilleece at the Peti Puk Restaurant?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember the conversation with Eileen Gilleece, and I believe the sentence was handed down after that conversation, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And did you understand that it was being suggested that you had invented the involvement of both of their clients and the security organs at the Main Staff, corps, and brigade level in the killing operation?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and particularly Mr. Bourgon understood that I was telling the truth when I was putting forth positions that are contrary to Mr. Obrenovic's statement and they're not targeting his client. And as for all of my other positions, he believed that they were a lie.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, I want to look at some sources of evidence, most of which were put to you in cross-examination, but I want to start with P107, please, the Krivaja 95 plan, for want of a better explanation, and we need to look at B/C/S page 5 and English page 7. Of course, you've seen that before, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: When you first saw it, did you read it all the way through?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And did you discover who was responsible for prisoners of war under Krivaja 95?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can read it in this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Could you read it out for us, please, so we have it in the record.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is 10(B), second paragraph: "Security organs and military police will determine the sectors where prisoners of war will be collected and secured, as well as the war booty. In treating the prisoners of war and the civilian population, you're strictly ordered to adhere to the provisions of the Geneva Conventions."

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And was that the position, as you understood it to be?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, I think everybody, with the exception possibly of Mr. Gosnell, who cross-examined you, referred you at some stage to the evidence of Miroslav Deronjic, which of course is admitted in this case under Rule 92 quater, and can we have now in e-court, please, P3139, which is under seal for reasons I don't understand, but there is a redacted version which is 3139A. And I don't believe any of the passages I'm going to refer to need to be prevented from broadcast, but if anybody's got any explanation or submissions to make, perhaps I'd welcome them now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Does anyone wish to make observations on this? None. So let's proceed, then. One moment. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, I'm told by Ms. Stewart that the reason that it was under seal was that apparently the testimony was in private session at some point, some of it was, and so that's why it's been limited in that way. And so 3139A is the one that's redacted, the private session testimony, and that was done a long time ago. Have we review that now, you know, we may be able to undo that if it's an issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are fine with remaining in open session, so let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you very much, and I thank Ms. Stewart and Mr. McCloskey for their help, as always.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: To be clear, because I think you ought to know what went on just now, I was reminded that there are two versions of the document. One is redacted and one not. The one which is not redacted is under seal, so we'll be making use of the redacted one, which then removes the obstruction that we might otherwise have. Thank you. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, let's hope this poses no problems. The P3139A, and I want to start at the bottom of page 87 and go to page 88. And it begins with a question from Mr. Karnavas: "On the 13th, you met with Mr. Beara, right, you had contact with him? "A. Correct." Can we go over the page, please: "And at that time, according to your testimony, Mr. Beara indicated that he was there to kill all of the Muslims that were there being warehoused in schools and in buses. Correct? "A. That's correct." Further down the page: "On the 13th, when Beara came to my office, I said literally what he conveyed to me, you know, how I acted. This is described in my interview. Up until that time in Bratunac, there was no systematic killing of people, except a major crime, an event, which happened in Kravica ..." And then the last paragraph: "On the 13th, in the evening, or the 14th, in the morning, prevented," I assume it must have been "I prevented Mr. Beara from committing any kind of killings, even systematic ones in Bratunac. According to the instructions of Karadzic, the way I interpreted it, the detainees were taken from Bratunac to Zvornik. So a large number of prisoners were alive on the 14th, and they were transported to Zvornik. On the 14th in the morning, I went to see Karadzic - I think you'll come to these questions - and I conveyed Mr. Beara's intentions the way he told them to Mr. Karadzic." Page 89: "Mr. Karadzic reacted -- please allow me to finish ..." I think he's talking to Mr. Karnavas there: "So allow me to explain that. Mr. Karadzic reacted the way he did, and I got the impression he was going to do something, and I returned to Bratunac. I did not have any particular information over those few days from Zvornik." Can we go to page 136, please. And halfway down the first question on that page: "I would like to refer to you of the evening of the 13th, and we're going to discuss that in the greatest of detail, but just as a way of example. You have testified on previous occasions, and there are some conflicting views, but you have testified nonetheless that you had had this meeting with Colonel Beara; correct? "A. Yes, of course it's correct. "Q. And you've said that Colonel Beara came there and said that he was going to kill all the prisoners in Bratunac; correct? "A. Correct. "Q. And you were able to exercise your authority to ensure that those killings did not take place in Bratunac; isn't that a fact? "A. Correct. "Q. And you, according to your testimony - if we are to believe your testimony - you were able to say, I have an order from President Karadzic, and I'm telling you, Colonel Beara, that there is not going to be any killings; correct? "A. Correct. "Q. And on the evening of the 13th before you went to bed in your safe and sound environment at home, you were under the impression that Colonel Beara had accepted the order that you had given him; correct? "A. Yes ..." And going down to the next question: "Now, on the morning of the 14th, you wake up or somebody wakes you up and you learn, according to your testimony, that Colonel Beara is searching for the brick factory in order to put some prisoners there; correct? "A. Correct, correct. "Q. And the brick factory happens to be in the Bratunac or within the Bratunac municipality? "A. Yes. "Q. Once again we see your de facto, if not de jure, powers, where you have a confrontation with Beara, and you order him out of Bratunac, that there shall be no killing in Bratunac; correct? "A. Correct." Can we go now to page 139, about halfway down, halfway -- Mr. Karnavas says: "Okay, I accept that, that you, in your position, had never heard of Beara. Fine. Now, you were able to have this confrontation, because it was somewhat confrontational, with Mr. Beara on the 14th of July, the head of a security organ of the VRS army. And you were to order him not to have any killings in Bratunac. Correct?" Two questions down: "All right. And in fact that is exactly what Beara did. He left angrily, according to you, according to your prior testimony; right? "A. Yes." And it goes on if we go to page 141, and he says halfway down that page: "But it's true that Beara acted in an angry manner, that he left the premises. I waited for a while and I realised that convoys were heading out to Zvornik." And then much further on, just to pages 298 and 299, again about halfway down the page, the middle of an answer: "Mr. Karnavas, after all it is an undisputable fact that Mr. Beara came to my office after my conversation with the president. That does not mean anything in itself, but it lends plausibility to what I stated. I agree with you that it is not fool-proof evidence. "Q. Okay. Since you mentioned that ..." He asked a question. "We talked about it. I didn't ask the questions directly. I just said, 'Mr. Beara I don't have any such orders. I did talk to President Karadzic, and I have orders of a different kind, but I didn't ask the question --" Over the page: "... in so many words. I have the conversation with Karadzic. After that, I received the visit of this gentleman, and I put two and two together." And lastly page 301, at the very bottom: "Q. And when you saw the president the next day, did you concretely and directly ask the president whether Beara was the one that he had ordered to come and grab or take the prisoners out of there so he could kill them or have them killed? "A. I said to Karadzic, word for word, Mr. Beara came to my offices, told me this and this. I didn't ask the question ..." Now, Mr. Pandurevic, that evidence was given in January 2004. When did you last read or hear about what Mr. Deronjic had said in evidence in the Blagojevic case?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I listened to this testimony upon my arrival at the Detention Unit in the second half of 2005, I believe, and that is when I was given the material from that trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: So that we're clear, did you know that Mr. Deronjic would or could give this account before you met with Dragan Obrenovic in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't know at all what Deronjic knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... or before you met Eileen Gilleece at the Peti Puk Restaurant?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. At that time, I also didn't know what Deronjic knew and what he was talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And obviously we've summarised his account of events in Bratunac on the 13th and 14th of July, but you've listened to it all. What kind of command structure can you identify in operation in relation to the prisoners in Bratunac on those dates?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In view of what we've heard from Mr. Deronjic's testimony, we can see that the order was not addressed to the Bratunac Brigade, but rather a man came with very specific orders, and whether he was given certain assets to be used in Bratunac or some other assets, I don't know. But at any rate, this wasn't in compliance with the usual chain of command that goes from the Main Staff via the corps and down to the brigade; rather, this chain of command started at the Main Staff, went via security organs who had the power and the authority from the Main Staff Command -- commander and carried out these tasks within their structures. Also, based on the powers and the authorisation that they had from the Main Staff commander, they had the right to engage the assets that they required for that operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we move on, please, and have 7D423 in e-court. And I think we'll just go straight to page 6 in the English, which is paragraph 10. Now, in May of 2003, Momir Nikolic entered a plea agreement with the Prosecution. When did you first learn of that fact?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw the statement of facts of Mr. Momir Nikolic here as part of the set of the material that was given to me at the Detention Unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'd like to object to the questions being put to the witness. This is not an issue that was raised, whether in any of the cross-examination conducted by -- whether the Prosecution or any of the Defence team. And I'm very well prepared to make an argument on to what is meant by matters arising to matters raised in cross-examination, if need be, but this is not an issue that was raised during cross-examination, and questions should not be permitted under re-examination in this regard. But if you need more argument, Mr. President, I'm pretty well ready to make all the submissions that are required for this purpose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's hear what Mr. Haynes has to say first. Yes, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would join to the objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: As do we, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: But of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: When you opened the number of doors in cross-examination that were opened by principally Mr. Bourgon, but secondly by Mr. Ostojic, you have to expect that people will go through those doors. And when you suggest to somebody that he has invented a whole account, starting in 1999 or 2000, and then in 2001, by reference to facts within his possession, it's perfectly proper, in re-examination, to point to features in the evidence in the case - and these are features in the evidence in the case - which he couldn't possibly have known about and which go to support the accuracy of his account. And that's really the purpose of doing all this. I can, in fact, probably refer to particular references to every piece of evidence I'm going to deal with. I've done this very carefully. But the principal point is this: You can't cross-examine a man in the way that Mr. Bourgon did and then say he's not entitled to come back and say, I can show you why what I'm saying is accurate, because it has a number of independent reference points I can point to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Don't rush. Mr. Bourgon first.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Well, indeed I'm going to ask for all the specific references my colleague is referring to, but I'd like to make this argument,

utterances.speaker: MR. PRESIDENT
utterances.text: There are a number of references which explain what is meant by "matters arising out of cross-examination." Now, the fact that this is the rule was highlighted by this Trial Chamber in its own order of 14 July 2006. It was also highlighted in the order setting out the guide-lines for the presentation of evidence and the conduct of the parties during the trial in Seselj case on 15 November 2007, that was at the annex paragraph 27. It was also raised on a number of occasions in the Blagojevic case, and I'd like to refer to something which was put by my colleague for the Prosecution in that case, talking about the limits of questions permitted in re-examination. My colleague said, and that was from Mr. McCloskey: "Mr. President, I think we need to be very strict upon that particular rule, because then it requires us to change our old viewpoint." And the Trial Chamber ruling on the same comments by Mr. McCloskey said: "Well, Mr. Karnavas, I think this Bench has warned you on many times before that redirect should be strictly within the cross-examination." Mr. President, as to the meaning to be given to the phrase "within the scope of cross-examination," I take this opportunity to raise the following references: I refer to "McWilliams, Canadian Criminal Evidence," 4th edition, Chapter 18..130 on re-examination. If I may quote from this text, it reads as follows: "The right to re-examine exists only when there has been cross-examination and must be confined to the explanation of matters arising thereon." Moving on a little further in the same paragraph: "Since counsel should elicit anything of relevance that a witness has to say on examination-in-chief, it follows that re-examination should be confined to matters arising from cross-examination." And there is, of course, one exception to this rule, which is very well known, and that is to allow counsel to adduce evidence as to matters they omitted on examination-in-chief by oversight, and this is -- the reason for this is obvious. It is because the object of the rule on limiting re-examination is to prevent counsel from intentionally putting their case in piecemeal, and that is not defeated when it's just to cover up an oversight. Now, this was a quote also in the McWilliams Canadian Criminal Cases evidence, and I can quote. That was from the Queen's case of 1820, and I would like to make that quote, which is -- no, sorry, I -- sorry, to "Archbold, 2006, Criminal Pleading Evidence and Practice," paragraph 8-247, and also citing from the same trial of Queen Carol Ann case, and I would like to cite this paragraph here: "There is a right in re-examination to ask all questions which may be proper to draw forth an explanation of the sense and meaning of the expressions used by the witness in cross-examination, if they be themselves doubtful, and also of the motif by which the witness was induced to use those expressions, but there is no right to go further and to introduce matters new in itself and not suited for the purpose of explaining either the expressions or motifs of the witness; Queen Carol Ann's case, 1820. Questions falling outside these limitations require, of course, the leave of the Judge." Moving on, Mr. President, in "Earl Levy, QC, Examination of Witnesses in Criminal Cases," 4th edition. I would like to quote from this case -- or from this book, and this is in Chapter 18 on re-examination. On the law, Earl Levy states: "When cross-examination is finished, opposing counsel may re-examine his or her witness to explain ambiguities, qualify admissions, or to put answers in cross-examination into proper perspective, and then a re-examination can be used only to explain or to qualify answers given in cross-examination, and no new material may be introduced unless with leave of the Court. In other words, re-examination is limited to what was raised in the cross-examination. However ..." And then we go to that same exception, which is matters which were forgotten as part of examination-in-chief with oversight. I can go on, Mr. President, to cite from McCormick on Evidence --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I object at this point. I think the Court is fully aware of this. It's been making decisions on this Rule for three years. We understand the role of Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is there anything you don't agree with so far, Mr. Haynes?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: No, and I'm just pleased to see I haven't taken them by surprise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. So let's stop here for today, because it's time. We'll pick on this -- I just put on record that you also wished to intervene, Mr. Ostojic, but that has to take place tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, one moment. I tried to see if we could shift the sitting from the afternoon to the morning tomorrow but we can't, so tomorrow afternoon at 2.15. Thank you.
